_We are committed to providing you with accurate, consistent and clear information to help you understand your rights and entitlements and your obligations._
_If you follow our information and it turns out to be incorrect, or it is misleading and you make a mistake as a result, we will take that into account when determining what action, if any, we should take._
_Some of the information in this Guide applies to a specific financial year. This is clearly marked. Make sure you have the information for the right year before making decisions based on that information._ | Answers to questions on: - [Working from home](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FWorkingfromhome%22&PiT=99991231235958#Workingfromhome) - [Work-related car expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FWorkrelatedcarexpenses%22&PiT=99991231235958#Workrelatedcarexpenses) - [Medicare levy surcharge](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FMedicarelevysurcharge%22&PiT=99991231235958#Medicarelevysurcharge) - [At home learning expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FAthomelearningexpenses%22&PiT=99991231235958#Athomelearningexpenses) - [Second job](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FSecondjob2%22&PiT=99991231235958#Secondjob2) - [Not an Australian resident, temporarily in Australia](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FNonresidentstemporarilyinAustraliaasares%22&PiT=99991231235958#NonresidentstemporarilyinAustraliaasares) - [Residents temporarily overseas](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FResidentstemporarilyoverseas1%22&PiT=99991231235958#Residentstemporarilyoverseas1) - [Financial hardship](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FFinancialhardship%22&PiT=99991231235958#Financialhardship) - [Buying protective items](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FBuyingprotectiveitems1%22&PiT=99991231235958#Buyingprotectiveitems1) - [Residential rental properties](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FResidentialrentalproperties%22&PiT=99991231235958#Residentialrentalproperties) - [Short-term rental properties](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FShorttermrentalproperties1%22&PiT=99991231235958#Shorttermrentalproperties1) ## Working from home **Question:** My employer is encouraging or requiring me to work from home. Will I be able to claim a deduction for home office expenses? **Answer:** Yes, if you work from home because of COVID-19 you may be able to claim a deduction for the additional running expenses you incur. These include expenses associated with heating, cooling and lighting in the area you are working from, phone and internet and other running expenses. We have introduced a temporary simplified method (shortcut method) for you to calculate the additional running expenses you incur as a result of working from home due to COVID-19. The shortcut method allows you to claim 80 cents for each hour you work from home and covers all deductible running expenses. Multiple people living in the same house can claim this new rate. For example, a couple living together could each individually claim the 80 cents per hour rate. You may still use one of the existing methods to calculate your running expenses if you would prefer to. This includes calculating your actual running expenses. **See also:** - [Employees working from home](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/COVID-19/Support-for-individuals-and-employees/Employees-working-from-home/) - [Home office expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/working-from-home-expenses/) . - Practical Compliance Guideline [PCG 2020/3](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22%3DCOG%2FPCG20203%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) _Claiming deductions for additional running expenses incurred whilst working from home due to COVID-19_ _This question was last updated on 9 April 2020._ **Question:** Can I claim working from home expenses when I'm on leave or if I've been stood down during the COVID-19 period? **Answer:** No, you can only claim for the actual time that you spend working from home due to COVID-19. Working from home does not include minimal tasks such as occasionally checking emails or taking calls. For example, if you have been stood down and you are occasionally receiving email updates from your employer about the situation, the time you spend checking those email updates will not be treated as time spent working from home. **See also:** - [Employees working from home](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/COVID-19/Support-for-individuals-and-employees/Employees-working-from-home/) - Practical Compliance Guideline [PCG 2020/3](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22COG%2FPCG20203%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) _Claiming deductions for additional running expenses incurred whilst working from home due to COVID-19_ _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** I worked from home before COVID-19 and my work pattern has not changed as a result. Am I entitled to claim the shortcut rate of 80 cents per work hour for my additional running expenses? **Answer:** Yes, the new shortcut method is intended to cover all taxpayers working from home between 1 March and 30 June 2020, whether the working arrangements are a result of COVID-19 or not. If you normally work from home, you can continue to claim your additional running expenses using one of the existing methods if you prefer: - the work-related portion of your actual expenses - the fixed rate of 52 cents per hour plus the work-related portion of expenses not covered by that rate. **See also:** - [Employees working from home](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/COVID-19/Support-for-individuals-and-employees/Employees-working-from-home/) - [Home office expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/working-from-home-expenses/) - Practical Compliance Guideline [PCG 2020/3](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22COG%2FPCG20203%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) _Claiming deductions for additional running expenses incurred whilst working from home due to COVID-19_ _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** If I use the shortcut method to claim my expenses while I work from home, what records do I need to keep? **Answer:** If you are using the shortcut method, you need to keep records showing the amount of time you have spent working from home. This could be in the form of timesheets, rosters, a diary or similar document that sets out the hours worked. _This question was last updated on 9 April 2020._ **Question:** If I claim my actual running expenses, what records do I need to keep? **Answer:** If you are claiming your actual running expenses, you need to retain receipts for expenses along with records showing your work-related use. Using [myDeductions](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/Online-services/Online-services-for-individuals-and-sole-traders/ATO-app/myDeductions/) in the ATO app is an easy and convenient way to keep your records in one place. **See also:** - [Employees working from home](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/COVID-19/Support-for-individuals-and-employees/Employees-working-from-home/) - [Home office expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/working-from-home-expenses/) _This question was last updated on 9 April 2020._ **Question:** Can I claim for my rent or mortgage and will this affect capital gains tax if I sell my house? **Answer:** Occupancy expenses relating to your home - such as rent, mortgage interest, property insurance and land taxes - will not become deductible merely because you are required to temporarily work from home due to COVID-19. People have asked whether working from home will disqualify them from claiming the main residence capital gains tax exemption when they sell their home. Because working from home in the current circumstances does not, in and of itself, create an entitlement to claim deductions for mortgage interest, you will not lose any part of the main residence exemption. **See also:** - [Home office expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/working-from-home-expenses/) - [Employees working from home](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/COVID-19/Support-for-individuals-and-employees/Employees-working-from-home/) - Practical Compliance Guideline [PCG 2020/3](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22COG%2FPCG20203%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) _Claiming deductions for additional running expenses incurred whilst working from home due to COVID-19_ _This question was last updated on 9 April 2020._ ## Work-related car expenses **Question:** I claim my car-related expenses using the logbook method. Will I need to keep a new logbook for an updated representative period of private and business usage during COVID-19? **Answer:** No, you are not required to keep a new logbook for the period in which your travel has been affected by COVID-19 as long as you account for any variation in the use of the car when working out your business kilometres and your business use percentage at the end of the income year. When working out your business kilometres at the end of the income year, you need to make a reasonable estimate based on any logbooks, odometer records or other records you have. In relation to the period in which your travel has been affected by COVID-19, you may keep a new logbook if you think it will provide a more accurate indication of your business use of the car. However if your overall business usage has not changed and you are merely using the car less, the odometer readings will reflect this and you will not need to keep another logbook. _This question was last updated on 8 May 2020._ ## Medicare levy surcharge **Question:** If I suspend my private health insurance due to losing my job and my income for Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS) purposes is above the threshold will I be liable for MLS? **Answer:** If you and all of your dependants were not covered by an [appropriate level of private patient hospital cover](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Private-health-insurance-rebate/#Appropriatelevelofprivatehospitalinsuran) , and your [income for MLS purposes](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Medicare-levy-surcharge/) is above a certain threshold, you may be required to pay the MLS. The rate of MLS depends on your income for MLS purposes. This applies unless you (and your dependents if you have them) are exempt from paying the Medicare levy (see [Surcharge exemption categories](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Tax-Return/2019/Tax-return/Medicare-levy-questions-M1-M2/M2-Medicare-levy-surcharge-(MLS)-2019/?=redirected_M2-MedicareLevySurcharge-redirect#Surchargeexemptioncategories) ). The base income threshold (under which you are not liable to pay the MLS) is $90,000 for singles and $180,000 for families (plus $1,500 for each dependent child after the first). However, you do not have to pay the MLS if your family income exceeds the threshold but your own income for MLS purposes was $22,801 or less. This amount was increased from $22,398 to $22,801 as part of the Government's economic response to COVID-19. If you are liable for the MLS, we will work it out based on the information you provide in your tax return. We will include it with your Medicare levy and it will show as one amount on your notice of assessment called Medicare levy and surcharge. If you want to calculate your Medicare levy surcharge, use the [Income tax estimator](https://www.ato.gov.au/calc_IncomeTaxEstimator) . **See also:** - [Medicare levy surcharge](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Medicare-levy-surcharge/) - [Income for Medicare levy surcharge purposes](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Medicare-levy-surcharge/#IncomeforMedicarelevysurchargepurposes1) - [Family and dependants for Medicare levy surcharge purposes](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Medicare-levy-surcharge/Family-and-dependants-for-Medicare-levy-surcharge-purposes/) _This question was last updated on 8 May 2020._ **Question:** If I lose my job and suspend my private health insurance part way through the year will I get a partial exemption from the Medicare levy surcharge, if my income for MLS purposes is above the threshold? **Answer:** If you hold hospital cover but temporarily suspend payments for that cover, then you may have to pay the MLS to account for the days that you did not hold the appropriate private patient hospital cover. This will be determined from the information that you provide in your tax return and that is supplied to the ATO by your private health insurance provider. If you were in an exemption category (see [Surcharge exemption categories](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Tax-Return/2019/Tax-return/Medicare-levy-questions-M1-M2/M2-Medicare-levy-surcharge-(MLS)-2019/?=redirected_M2-MedicareLevySurcharge-redirect#Surchargeexemptioncategories) ) for the whole of the year then you do not have to pay the surcharge. **See also:** - [Medicare levy surcharge](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Medicare-levy-surcharge/) - [Income thresholds and rates for the Medicare levy surcharge](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Medicare-levy-surcharge/Medicare-levy-surcharge-income,-thresholds-and-rates/) - [Private health insurance rebate](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Private-health-insurance-rebate/) - [Appropriate level of private hospital insurance](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Medicare-and-private-health-insurance/Private-health-insurance-rebate/) _This question was last updated on 8 May 2020._ ## At home learning expenses **Question:** I am a working parent with school-aged children who are learning from home during the COVID-19 crisis. Will I be able to claim a deduction for the costs associated with setting them up for learning? **Answer:** No, costs relating to your children's education are personal expenses and not deductible. Examples of costs include: - setting them up to do online learning - teaching them at home - purchasing school supplies or items like desks, iPads, or sporting equipment. If you are an employee who is working from home, you can only claim a deduction for expenses that are directly related to your work. **See also:** - [Employees working from home](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/COVID-19/Support-for-individuals-and-employees/Employees-working-from-home/) - [Home office expenses](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals/income-deductions-offsets-and-records/deductions-you-can-claim/working-from-home-expenses/) . _This question was last updated on 17 April 2020._ ## Second job **Question:** I have lost my job as a result of COVID-19 and have found another job. Will I be taxed at a higher rate because it is considered a second job? **Answer:** No, if you have lost your job, then you are entitled to claim the [tax free threshold](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Jobs-and-employment-types/Working-as-an-employee/Income-from-more-than-one-job/#Howtoclaimthetaxfreethreshold) to reduce the amount of tax that is withheld from your pay from your new job. Second jobs usually have a higher amount of tax withheld from your pay because you already have another job from which you are earning income and are claiming the tax-free threshold. Withholding at a higher rate reduces the likelihood of you having a tax debt at the end of the income year. When you start your new job, your employer will give you a tax file number declaration to complete. Centrelink is also a payer and they will give you this form if you apply for their payments. You tell your new employer that you want to claim the tax-free threshold by answering 'Yes' at question 8 'Do you want to claim the tax-free threshold from this payer?' You do not have to claim the tax-free threshold if you want a higher amount of tax withheld from your pay. You can see how much tax you employer will withhold from your payment by using the tax withheld calculator. Find out about: - [Tax withheld calculator](https://www.ato.gov.au/Calculators-and-tools/Tax-withheld-calculator) - [Claiming the tax-free threshold](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Jobs-and-employment-types/Working-as-an-employee/Income-from-more-than-one-job/#Howtoclaimthetaxfreethreshold) - How much tax you employer will withhold from your payment - [Tax withheld calculator](https://www.ato.gov.au/Calculators-and-tools/Tax-withheld-calculator/) _This question was last updated on 9 April 2020._ ## Not an Australian resident, temporarily in Australia **Question:** I am not an Australian resident. I am staying in Australia for longer than I expected because of COVID-19. What are my Australian tax obligations? **Answer:** If you are not an Australian resident for tax purposes, you will be assessable only on income from an Australian source subject to the application of any applicable Australian double tax agreements (see the [question on double tax agreements](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FDoubletaxagreement%22&PiT=99991231235958#Doubletaxagreement) ). You may need to lodge an Australian tax return if you earn any assessable income from an Australian source. This includes salary or wage income that is assessable in Australia(see the questions on employment income concerning leave and salary and wages below). Your Australian tax obligations will otherwise generally remain unchanged. You may need to lodge an Australian tax return if you become an Australian resident for tax purposes. As an Australian resident all Australian-sourced income, including salary or wage income and investment income, will be assessable. All foreign-sourced income will also be assessable unless you are an Australian resident who is a temporary resident. **See also:** - [International tax for individuals](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Coming-to-Australia-or-going-overseas/) - [Do you need to lodge a tax return?](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/your-tax-return/Before-you-prepare-your-tax-return/Work-out-if-you-need-to-lodge-a-tax-return/) _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** Will my tax residency for tax purposes change as a result of me returning to Australia due to COVID-19? **Answer:** Whether you are a resident for tax purposes in Australia is a question of fact that requires consideration of your circumstances. If you are here temporarily for some weeks or months because of COVID-19 then you will not become an Australian resident for tax purposes provided you: - usually live overseas permanently - intend to return there as soon as you are able to. However the tax residency issue may be more complicated if you: - end up staying in Australia for a lengthy period - do not plan to return to your country of residency when you are able to do so. We appreciate that there will be unique situations with a range of potential tax outcomes. We will update and may revise this advice progressively as events unfold. **See also:** - [International tax for individuals - Working out your tax residency](https://www.ato.gov.au/Calculators-and-tools/Work-out-your-tax-residency/) - Taxation Ruling [TR 98/17](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22TXR%2FTR9817%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) _Income tax: residency status of individuals entering Australia_ - Taxation Ruling [IT 2650](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22ITR%2FIT2650%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) _Income tax: residency - permanent place of abode outside Australia_ _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** What happens if I earn employment income that is paid leave while I am in Australia temporarily? **Answer:** If you usually work overseas and earn foreign-source employment income and you have been on leave since arriving in Australia, the income you receive from your foreign employer for paid leave (such as annual or holiday leave) is not from an Australian source so you do not need to declare it in Australia. _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** What happens if I earn employment income that is salary and wages from continuing my foreign employment (working remotely) while I am in Australia temporarily? **Answer:** Whether employment income you earn is assessable depends on whether it is from an Australian or a foreign source. It also depends on whether a double tax agreement applies (see the [question on double tax agreements](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FDoubletaxagreement%22&PiT=99991231235958#Doubletaxagreement) ). The source of income always depends on the facts. Usually the place where the employment is exercised is very significant when deciding the source of employment income (salary or wages). However, in certain circumstances other factors may be more significant. COVID-19 has created a special set of circumstances that must be taken into account when considering the source of the employment income of a non-resident who usually works overseas but instead performs that same employment in Australia as a result of COVID-19. In this situation, we accept that, if the working arrangement is short term (three months or less), the employment income will not have an Australian source. * * * **Example: Short term working arrangement for three-month period** _Eric is a financial advisor who came to Australia for a holiday on 20 December 2019, intending to leave at the end of January 2020. Eric decided not to leave Australia because of COVID-19 but intended to return to his usual country of residence as soon as it was safe to do so. He started working remotely in Australia on 1 February doing the same things he would normally do in his country of residence for his foreign employer._ _The three-month period starts on 1 February 2020 and ends on 30 April 2020. It does not matter if Eric is a full-time or part-time employee. Eric's employment income for this three-month period will not be considered to have an Australian source._ * * * For working arrangements that last longer than three months, all your facts and circumstances will need to be examined to determine if your employment is connected to Australia. This includes whether: - the terms and conditions of your employment contract change - the nature of your employment activities change - you commence performing some work for an Australian entity affiliated with your employer - the economic impact or result of your work shifts to Australia - your economic employer - the entity to which you are providing your services - is in Australia (see Taxation Ruling [TR 2013/1](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22TXR%2FTR20131%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) ) - you perform work with Australian clients - the performance of your work is otherwise wholly or to a significant degree dependent upon you being physically present in Australia to complete it - Australia becomes your permanent place of work - your intention towards Australia changes. In some limited situations your employment income may not have an Australian source. This may be the case if all of the following apply: - The only thing that has changed about your employment is that you are now doing it from Australia as a result of COVID-19. - There are no other connections to Australia. - You intend to leave Australia as soon as you are able to do so. * * * **Example: Circumstances of employment change to an Australian source** _Jane is an IT professional residing overseas servicing software applications for her employer. She is able to undertake these tasks remotely from anywhere in the world. On 1 March 2020 she decides to return to Australia temporarily as a result of COVID-19, continuing to work exclusively for her foreign employer from Australia for as long as she is able. Everything else about her employment remains unchanged until 1 May 2020, when, due to a shortage of work with her foreign employer, she begins to also undertake similar work for a related Australian entity. In relation to the Australian work, she is assigned work by, and reports to, an Australian manager._ _The employment income Jane derives between 1 March and 30 April 2020 is foreign sourced as it is not connected to Australia._ _The employment income Jane derives from 1 May 2020 is Australian sourced due to the change in her employment circumstances._ _From 1 May 2020, Jane's employment income is assessable to her in Australia, subject to the application of the 183 day exception, which is explained in the_ _[question on double tax agreements](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22SAV%2FCOVID19-FAQ%2FDoubletaxagreement%22&PiT=99991231235958#Doubletaxagreement)_ _._ * * * **See also:** - Taxation Ruling [TR 2013/1](https://www.ato.gov.au/law/view/document?LocID=%22TXR%2FTR20131%2FNAT%2FATO%22&PiT=99991231235958) _Income tax: the identification of 'employer' for the purposes of the short-term visit exception under the Income from Employment Article, or its equivalent, of Australia's tax treaties_ _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** What if I get a wage or salary in Australia and my home country has a double tax agreement with Australia? **Answer:** Australia's [double tax agreements](https://treasury.gov.au/tax-treaties/income-tax-treaties) (DTA) provide that, in certain circumstances, employment income derived by a person who is a resident of the other country (after applying the DTA tie-breaker rules) from performing employment duties in Australia for a short period will not be taxed in Australia. Each DTA must be checked carefully as the wording, conditions and time periods vary from DTA to DTA. Generally, employment income will not be taxed in Australia if: - you are a resident of a country with which Australia has a DTA (the DTA country) - you are not present in Australia for more than 183 days in aggregate in either an income year or a 12-month period (depending on the applicable DTA) - your salary and wages are paid to you by, or on behalf of, an employer that is not a resident of Australia - your salary and wages are not deductible against the profits of an Australian permanent establishment of your employer. For some DTAs, the 183 days do not necessarily all have to be in the same income year, and there may be breaks in the aggregate. * * * **Example: accumulation of more than 183 days** _Ian spent the following time in Australia:_ - _15 December 2019 to 3 January 2020 (20 days)_ - _10 March 2020 to 1 October 2020 (176 days)_ _As Ian's period of time in Australia exceeds 183 days, the DTA does not apply to prevent Australia from taxing Ian's salary or wages from an Australian source in the 2019-20 and 2020-21 income years._ * * * **See also:** - [Double Tax Agreement countries](https://treasury.gov.au/tax-treaties/income-tax-treaties) _This question was last updated on 9 April 2020._ ## Residents temporarily overseas **Question:** I am working overseas because of COVID-19. What are my Australian tax obligations? **Answer:** If you usually live and work in Australia but you are temporarily overseas as a result of COVID-19, there is no change to your Australian tax obligations. If you are required to pay foreign income tax overseas, a foreign income tax offset will ordinarily apply to reduce your Australian tax payable. _This question was last updated on 20 March 2020._ ## Financial hardship **Question:** Under the COVID-19 early release of super arrangements, can I make more than one application in the same financial year as long as I don't withdraw more than $10,000 in total in either the 2019-20 or 2020-21 financial years? **Answer:** No. From now until 30 June 2020, a member can make one application for a determination in the 2019-20 financial year, up to $10,000. From 1 July 2020 to 24 September 2020, a member can make one application for a determination in the 2020-21 financial year, up to $10,000. A member who requests an amount of less than $10,000 in their application in either financial year cannot make a subsequent application in the same financial year, even if it is an application to release the difference between the originally requested amount and the $10,000 limit. **See also:** - [COVID-19 early release of super](https://www.ato.gov.au/About-ATO/Research-and-statistics/In-detail/Super-statistics/Early-release/COVID-19-Early-release-of-super/) _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** I am a temporary resident. Can I access my super under the COVID-19 early access arrangements? **Answer:** It depends on your situation. Certain eligible temporary residents can apply to access up to $10,000 of their super until 30 June 2020. Otherwise, if you have worked and earned super while visiting Australia on a temporary visa, you can apply to have this super paid to you as a departing Australia superannuation payment (DASP) after you leave. **See also:** - [Temporary residents and super](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Super/Temporary-residents-and-superannuation/) - [Departing Australia Superannuation Payment (DASP](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Super/Temporary-residents-and-superannuation/Departing-Australia-superannuation-payment-DASP/) ) _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** I've had my hours cut back at work and I can't afford to pay the bills. What assistance is available to me? **Answer:** You can apply to have the tax withheld from your pay reduced for the rest of the financial year. This means you don't have to wait to get a refund when you lodge your tax return. If you are considering this, you need to lodge a variation form - and you need to know: - The variation will apply for the remainder of the financial year. - The last date for lodgment of your variation application for the current year is 30 April 2020. - If the amounts withheld do not cover your actual tax liabilities at the end of the year, you will have to pay the balance in your annual tax return. - You cannot get a variation if any of the following apply - Your tax returns are not up to date. - You have a debit assessment for the previous year as a result of a previous withholding variation. - You have outstanding tax or superannuation debts. If you want to apply for a variation, you can lodge your application online: - [PAYG withholding variation application (e-variation)](https://www.ato.gov.au/forms/payg-withholding-variation-application/) The JobKeeper payment is open to eligible employers to enable them to pay their eligible employee's salary or wages. If you and your employer are eligible and your employer is participating in the JobKeeper Payment scheme, they would be required to pay you a minimum of $1,500 (before tax) per fortnight. **See also:** - Eligibility - [JobKeeper Payment](https://www.ato.gov.au/general/JobKeeper-Payment/) _This question was last updated on 17 April 2020._ **Question:** My income has decreased due to the downturn in the economy and I can't afford to pay my expenses. Can I access my super? **Answer:** You may be allowed to withdraw some of your super on compassionate grounds to help deal with the adverse economic effects of COVID-19. From mid-April you will be able to apply online through myGov to access up to $10,000 of your superannuation before 1 July 2020. You will also be able to apply to access up to a further $10,000 from 1 July 2020 until 24 September 2020. To apply for early release, you must satisfy one or more of the following requirements: - You are unemployed. - You are eligible to receive a job seeker payment, youth allowance for jobseekers, parenting payment (which includes the single and partnered payments), special benefit or farm household allowance. - On or after 1 January 2020, any of the following happened - You were made redundant. - Your working hours were reduced by 20% or more. - You were a sole trader and your business was suspended or your turnover decreased by 20% or more. The amount of super released early under these circumstances will not be included in your assessable income. **See also:** - [Early access to your super](https://www.ato.gov.au/Individuals/Super/Withdrawing-and-using-your-super/Early-access-to-super/) - [Financial difficulties and serious hardship](https://www.ato.gov.au/General/Support-to-lodge-and-pay/Tax-Support/Tax-support-for-individuals/) - Treasury's pages [Supporting individuals and households](https://treasury.gov.au/coronavirus/households) _This question was last updated on 27 March 2020._ ## Buying protective items **Question:** Can I claim a deduction for gloves, face masks, sanitiser, anti-bacterial spray that I use at work due to COVID-19? **Answer:** You may be able to claim a deduction for protective items you purchase and use at work. To be deductible both of the following must apply: - You must have incurred the expense yourself. - It must have a sufficient connection with the earning of your assessable income, which means - you are exposed to the risk of illness or injury in the course of carrying out your income earning activities - the risk is not remote or negligible - the protective item is of a kind that provides protection from that risk and would reasonably be expected to be used in the circumstances - you use the item in the course of carrying out your income earning activities. If your specific employment duties require you to have physical contact or be in close proximity to customers or clients while carrying out your duties or you are involved in cleaning premises, you can claim a deduction for expenditure on protective items. Examples of this type of work include the: - medical industry (such as doctors, nurses, dentists and allied health workers) - cleaning industry - airline industry - hairdressing and beautician industry - retail, caf é and restaurant industry. If you work in these industries or occupations, the risk is not remote or negligible. If you use items for both work-related and private purposes, you can only claim a deduction for the portion of the expense that relates to your work-related use. _This question was last updated on 20 March 2020._ ## Residential rental properties **Question:** My tenants are not paying their full rent or have temporarily stopped paying rent because their income has been adversely affected by COVID-19. Can I still claim deductions on my rental property expenses? **Answer:** Yes. If tenants are not meeting their payment obligations under the lease agreement due to COVID-19 and you continue to incur normal expenses on your property, then you will still be able to claim these expenses in your tax return. _This question was last updated on 3 April 2020._ **Question:** I'm considering reducing the rent for tenants whose income has been adversely affected by COVID-19 to enable them to stay in the property. The tenants are not in default of their rent. Will my deduction for rental property expenses be reduced because of this? **Answer:** No. If you decide to reduce the rent to enable your tenants to remain in the property (thereby maximising your rental return in a changed rental market), your deduction for rental property expenses will not be reduced. _This question was last updated on 3 April 2020._ **Question:** If I receive a back payment of rent or an amount of insurance for lost rent, is this amount assessable income? **Answer:** Yes. These amounts should be declared as income in the tax year in which you receive the amounts. _This question was last updated on 3 April 2020._ **Question:** If the bank defers loan repayments for a period of time as a result of COVID-19, can I continue to claim interest on the loan as a deduction? **Answer:** Yes. If interest continues to accumulate on your loan, it will be an expense that you have incurred and is therefore deductible. Interest remains deductible on the loan even if the bank defers the repayments. _This question was last updated on 3 April 2020._ **Question:** Can I access the new instant asset write-off for my property? **Answer:** No. If you are a property investor, you cannot access the instant asset write-off deduction. **See also:** - [Instant asset write-off deduction](https://www.ato.gov.au/Business/Depreciation-and-capital-expenses-and-allowances/Simpler-depreciation-for-small-business/Instant-asset-write-off/) _This question was last updated on 3 April 2020._ ## Short-term rental properties **Question:** COVID-19 is adversely affecting demand, including cancellation of existing bookings, for a property that I currently rent out as short-term accommodation. I have previously had some private use of the property. Will I be able to continue to deduct expenses associated with this property in the same proportion as I was entitled to claim before COVID-19 for the period that demand is adversely affected? **Answer:** The amount you can claim will depend on how the property had been used before COVID-19 and how you had planned to use it during the COVID-19 period. If the reason for the adverse effect on demand for your property is because of COVID-19 (or the bushfires before this), you can continue to deduct expenses associated with your property in the same proportion as you were entitled to deduct before COVID-19. If you had started to use the property in a different way than before COVID-19, the proportion of expenses you can claim as a deduction may change. Examples of changed use include: - increased private use of the property by you, your family or your friends - a decision to permanently stop renting out your property once the COVID-19 restrictions end. _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** I would like to stop paying for advertising on my short-term rental property during COVID-19 as I am not getting any queries for the property. Can I still claim deductions associated with holding the property? **Answer:** It depends on a wider range of factors, not just one. Whether active and bona fide efforts are made to ensure a property is available for rent is only one factor to consider when determining the appropriate method to apportion deductions for a short-term rental property. You would need to consider how the property had been used before COVID-19 and how you plan to use it during the period now adversely affected by COVID-19. During this time we acknowledge it may be a reasonable commercial decision to temporarily reduce the level of paid advertising for your property, depending on the restrictions in your property's locality. However this factor alone doesn't necessarily determine the allowable proportion of your deductions. _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ **Question:** I am using my holiday home privately for myself and my family so we can isolate during COVID-19. Can I continue to claim deductions for the property for this period, as I am unable to rent the property commercially? **Answer:** No. If you are using the property yourself or providing it to friends or family, this will increase your private usage of the property and reduce the deductions you can claim. _This question was last updated on 23 April 2020._ * * * **© AUSTRALIAN TAXATION OFFICE FOR THE COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA** You are free to copy, adapt, modify, transmit and distribute this material as you wish (but not in any way that suggests the ATO or the Commonwealth endorses you or any of your services or products). **ATO references:** NO COVID-19 FAQ * * * **Copyright notice** © Australian Taxation Office for the Commonwealth of Australia You are free to copy, adapt, modify, transmit and distribute material on this website as you wish (but not in any way that suggests the ATO or the Commonwealth endorses you or any of your services or products). correctness.justification: Substance matches the reference throughout: salary/rent as ordinary income under s 6-5, capital gain as statutory income under Part 3-1 (with a correct 50% Division 115 discount to $120,000), Australian source for leave pay, full-year residence under s 6(1), and FRE 4 producing a $213.01 gain assessable under s 775-15 — with correct figures for the period. Minor slips only: the gain mechanism is cited to s 775-55(3) (gain is s 775-55(2)), the 10/12 salary proration ignores two December days, and the s 8-1 deduction-translation point goes beyond the reference; the absence of captured support is penalised in the audit dimensions, not here.

completeness.justification: Covers all four parts and exceeds the reference in places (business income, FX gain in (a), deduction effect in (d)), but omits the source of the rental income (the Nathan v FCT limb of (b)) and the capital-receipt characterisation; cases are named but no leading judgment is engaged with a quoted passage, capping this at 3.

faithfulness.justification: Only the part (b) source principle is even partially verifiable from captured text ([[5]] contains 'the place where the employment is exercised is very significant' and the paid-leave Q&A); all seven legislation citations ([[1]]-[[4]], [[6]]-[[8]]) returned 'page neither read nor found', and the cases (French, Efstathakis, Applegate, Joachim) have no source entries at all — well under 25% of load-bearing claims verified.

helpfulness.justification: Well-structured part-by-part answer pitched at a professional with clear FX workings, but it nowhere sets out the governing statutory words verbatim and offers no closing next step — two of the three working elements level 3 requires, so per the ladder it falls to 2.

citation_grounding.justification: Citations are relevant and properly claim-anchored to the correct ITAA provisions, but every statutory proposition rests on an unverified capture (7 of 8 pages empty); the only captured source is secondary ATO guidance partially supporting a common-law sourcing point, and several named cases have no source entry — squarely level 3 ('material claims rest on unverified captures').

judge_output.summary: Substantively strong — right conclusions, sections and figures on all four parts — but the audit trail largely fails: 7 of 8 cited legislation pages have no captured text, no statutory words are quoted, and the case authorities have no source entries.

(2) You dispose of a \\* CGT asset if a change of [ownership](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) occurs from you to another entity, whether because of some act or event or by operation of law. However, a change of [ownership](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) does not occur if you stop being the legal [owner](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) of the asset but continue to be its beneficial [owner](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner). Note: A change in the [trustee](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of a trust does not constitute a change in the entity that is the [trustee](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of the trust (see [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.40.html#subsection)960 - 100(2)). This means that CGT event A1 [will](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#will) not happen merely because of a change in the [trustee](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee). (3) The time of the event is: (a) when you enter into the contract for the \\* disposal; or (b) if there is no contract--when the change of [ownership](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) occurs. Example: In June 1999 you enter into a contract to sell land. The contract is settled in October 1999. You [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital gain of $50,000. The gain is made in the 1998 \- 99 [income year](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) (the year you entered into the contract) and not the 1999 \- 2000 [income year](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) (the year that settlement takes place). Note 1: If the contract falls through before completion, this event does not happen because no change in [ownership](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner) occurs. Note 2: If the asset was compulsorily acquired from you: see [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.40.html#subsection)(6). (4) You [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital gain if the \\* capital proceeds from the disposal are more than the asset's \\* cost base. You [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital loss if those capital proceeds are less than the asset's \\* [reduced cost base](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#reduced_cost_base). Exceptions (5) A \\* capital gain or \\* capital loss you [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) is disregarded if: (a) you \\* acquired the asset before 20 September 1985; or (b) for a lease that you granted: (i) it was granted before that day; or (ii) if it has been renewed or extended--the start of the last renewal or extension occurred before that day. Note 1: You can [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a gain if you dispose of [shares](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share) in a company, or an interest in a trust, that you acquired before that day: see CGT event K6. Note 2: A capital gain or loss you [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) because you assign a right [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) or in relation to a [general insurance policy](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#general_insurance_policy) you [held](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#held) with an [HIH company](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#hih_company) to the Commonwealth, the [trustee](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#trustee) of the [HIH Trust](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#hih_trust) or a prescribed entity is also disregarded: see section 322 \- 15\. Note 3: A capital gain or loss made by a demerging entity from CGT event A1 happening as a result of a demerger is also disregarded: see section [125](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s125.html)\- [155](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s155.html). Note 4: A capital gain or loss you [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) because of section [16AI](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ba195972/s16ai.html) of the [Banking Act 1959](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ba195972/)is disregarded: see section 253 \- 10 of [this Act](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#this_act). Section [16AI](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ba195972/s16ai.html) of the [Banking Act 1959](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ba195972/): (a) reduces your right to be paid an amount by an ADI [in connection with](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#in_connection_with) an account to the extent of your entitlement [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) Division 2AA of [Part](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part)II of that Act to be paid an amount by APRA; and (b) [provides](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#provide) that, to the extent of the reduction, the right becomes a right of APRA. Note 5: A capital gain or loss you [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) because, [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section [62ZZL](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ia1973116/s62zzl.html) of the [Insurance Act 1973](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ia1973116/), you dispose of a CGT asset consisting of your rights against a [general insurance company](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#general_insurance_company) to APRA is disregarded: see section 322 \- 30 of [this Act](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#this_act). Compulsory acquisition (6) If the asset was \\* acquired from you by an entity [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) a power of compulsory acquisition conferred by an \\* Australian law or a \* foreign law, the time of the event is the earliest of: (a) when you received compensation from the entity; or (b) when the entity became the asset's [owner](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#owner); or (c) when the entity entered it [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) that power; or (d) when the entity took possession [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) that power. (2) The time of the event is: (a) when you enter into the contract that results in the asset ending; or (b) if there is no contract--when the asset ends. (3) You [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital gain if the \\* capital proceeds from the ending are more than the asset's \\* cost base. You [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) a capital loss if those capital proceeds are less than the asset's \\* [reduced cost base](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#reduced_cost_base). Note: The capital proceeds referred to in this [subsection](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.40.html#subsection) are reduced if the gain or loss was for [shares](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share) and an amount was taken into account as a capital gain for the [shares](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share) [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) former section 160ZL of the [Income Tax Assessment Act 1936](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1936240/)for the 1997 \- 98 [income year](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) or an earlier [income year](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year): see section 104 \- 25 of the [Income Tax (Transitional Provisions) Act 1997](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itpa1997402/). (4) A lease is taken to have expired even if it is extended or renewed. Exceptions (5) A \\* capital gain or \\* capital loss you [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) is disregarded if: (a) you \\* acquired the asset before 20 September 1985; or (b) for a lease that you granted: (i) it was granted before that day; or (ii) if it has been renewed or extended--the start of the last renewal or extension occurred before that day. Note 1: There are other exceptions if: • your lease expires and you did not use it mainly to produce assessable income: see section 118 \- 40; or • you exercise rights to acquire [shares](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share) or units: see section 130 \- 40; or • you acquire [shares](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share) or units by converting a convertible interest: see section 130 \- 60; or • you exercise an option: see section 134 \- 1\. Note 2: A company can agree to forgo any capital loss it [makes](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) as a result of forgiving a commercial debt owed to it by another company where the companies are [under common ownership](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under_common_ownership): see section [245](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s245.html)\- 90\. Note 3: A capital gain or loss a company [makes](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) because [shares](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#share) in its 100% [subsidiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#subsidiary) are cancelled (an example of CGT event C2) on the liquidation of the [subsidiary](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#subsidiary) may be reduced if there was a roll \- [over](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#over) for a CGT asset [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) Subdivision 126 \- B: see section 126 \- [85](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s85.html). Note 5: Cost base adjustments are made only [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) Subdivision 125 \- B if there is a roll \- [over](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#over) [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) that Subdivision for CGT event C2 happening as a result of a demerger. Note 6: A capital gain or loss made by a demerging entity from CGT event C2 happening as a result of a demerger is also disregarded: see section [125](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s125.html)\- [155](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s155.html). Note 7: A capital gain or loss you [make](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) from the meeting of your entitlement [under](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) Division 2AA (Financial claims [scheme](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#scheme) for account - [holders](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#holder) with insolvent ADIs) of [Part](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part)II of the [Banking Act 1959](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ba195972/)or [Part](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#part)VC (Financial claims [scheme](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#scheme) for account \- [holders](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#holder) with insolvent general insurers) of the [Insurance Act 1973](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ia1973116/)is disregarded: see sections 253 \- 10 and 322 \- 30 of [this Act](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#this_act). * * * **AustLII:** [Copyright Policy](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/austlii/copyright.html) **\|** [Disclaimers](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/austlii/disclaimers.html) **\|** [Privacy Policy](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/austlii/privacy.html) **\|** [Feedback](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/austlii/feedback.html)

    extract (page read): ## [![](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/images/tiny-austlii.gif)](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/) Commonwealth Consolidated Acts \[ [Index](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/)\] \[ [Table](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/index.html#s104.110)\] \[ [Search](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinoform.pl)\] \[ [Search this Act](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinoform.pl/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/)\] \[ [Notes](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/notes.html)\] \[ [Noteup](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinosrch.pl?query=cth+consol_act+itaa1997240+s104.110)\] \[ [Previous](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s104.107h.html)\] \[ [Next](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s104.115.html)\] \[ [Download](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/download.cgi/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240)\] \[ [Help](https://classic.austlii.edu.au/help/legis-help.html)\] * * * ### INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1997 - SECT 104.110 **Granting a lease: CGT event F1** (1) CGT event F1 happens if a lessor grants, renews or extends a lease. Note 1: Other CGT events can apply to leases. An assignment of a lease is an example of CGT event A1. correctness.justification: Every conclusion matches the reference: (a) C1, 9 April 2023 (s 104-20(2)(a) first receipt of compensation); (b) A1, 1 March 2023 (s 104-10(3)(b), no contract); (c) C2, 4 December 2022 (s 104-25(2)(a)); (d) F1 for Chen, 3 May 2020 (s 104-110(2)(a)(i)) — each stated from the legislation itself. Minor uncited assertions (the hedged personal-use-asset/collectable comment, and rent being ordinary income under s 6-5) go beyond what the captured sources bear out, barring level 5.

completeness.justification: The core of each scenario is covered, but a key point in the reference is missing: the lease expiry on 2 May 2023 triggering CGT event C2 for Donna (the lessee), entitling her to a capital loss — significant because the question deliberately supplies the expiry date. The reference's subsidiary point that C1 (not A1) is the more apt event in (a) is also not engaged, and no case authority (e.g., on contract timing) is referred to.

faithfulness.justification: All eight core determinations are anchored at the claim to the correct section and verified from the captured operative text (s 104-20(1),(2)(a); s 104-10(1)–(3); s 104-25(1),(2)(a); s 104-110(1),(2)(a)(i)), with the timing rules quoted nearly verbatim; however, the contract-law reasoning in (b) ('verbal promise lacks consideration', 'real property requires a written instrument') and the s 6-5 rent characterisation in (d) are legal propositions asserted without any citation, so a reviewer cannot audit the whole answer without leaving the page.

helpfulness.justification: Well-organised per-scenario with governing statutory words set out and clear application, but it has no concrete closing next step (e.g., market value substitution under s 116-30 for the gift, or cost-base/collectable threshold checks), which the ladder requires for level 3; it also stops short on (d) by not addressing the lease-expiry consequences.

citation_grounding.justification: Dense, claim-level anchoring to the primary legislation with full operative text captured: every CGT event and timing rule is verified word-for-word from the AustLII captures of ss 104-10, 104-20, 104-25 and 104-110, with no irrelevant citations. A small minority of claims rest on nothing — the uncited s 6-5 ordinary-income proposition and the contract-law assertions in (b) — preventing level 5's requirement that every material statutory proposition be grounded in captured text.

judge_output.summary: All four primary determinations (C1, A1, C2, F1) and dates are correct and claim-anchored to the captured statutory text, but the answer omits the reference's second limb in (d) — CGT event C2 for Donna on lease expiry (2 May 2023) — and carries minor uncited legal assertions.

correctness.justification: Three limbs are right — the $650,000 base under s 116-20(1), +$200,000 under the s 116-55 assumption-of-liability rule, and −$20,000 under the s 116-50(1)(b) repaid rule — but the candidate entirely misses s 116-60 (misappropriation by an employee or agent), instead reasoning via s 116-45 and s 103-10 that the assistant's theft does not reduce proceeds. That is a material, outcome-determinative error contradicting the reference: the final figure of $830,000 is wrong; the correct capital proceeds are $780,000.

completeness.justification: Covers the general rule, the assumption-of-liability modification and the repaid-rule modification, and engages with the stolen-cash fact, with the computation shown as a table. But one of the reference's four key limbs — the s 116-60 misappropriation reduction of $50,000 — is absent (replaced by an incorrect non-receipt/constructive-receipt analysis), so the final computation and its governing rule are missing; no case-law engagement was required on these facts.

faithfulness.justification: Most load-bearing claims are anchored at the claim and verified by captured text: s 116-20(1)(a)-(b) [[1]], s 116-55 plus its mortgage example [[2]], s 116-45's conditions [[3]], s 103-10(1)'s "applied for your benefit … or as you direct" [[4]], and s 116-50(1)(b) with its misrepresentation example [[5]] all check out. Deductions: the claim that s 116-45 "only applies when the purchaser defaults" goes beyond the captured conditions (a)-(c), the negative conclusion that nothing reduces the stolen $50,000 cannot be verified from the cited captures (the governing s 116-60 is absent), and the aside about a "separate capital loss" against the assistant is unanchored — roughly 80-90% verified.

helpfulness.justification: Strong form for a professional: step-by-step structure, each component tied to a section, and a workings table laying out the computation. However, the governing statutory words are mostly paraphrased rather than set out (only "as you direct" is quoted) and there is no concrete closing next step (e.g. read s 116-60, or check recovery/insurance against the assistant), so it does not meet every level-3 working element; judged on form only, per the rubric, its wrong figure is not held against it here.

citation_grounding.justification: All five citations are primary legislation (ITAA 1997 ss 116-20, 116-55, 116-45, 103-10, 116-50) anchored at the specific claims they support, and every capture contains the full operative section text — not teasers or tables of contents — so the base rule, mortgage uplift and termite-settlement reduction are fully auditable from the page. Held back from 5 because the conclusion-determinative claim (that the stolen $50,000 is not deductible) rests on ss 116-45 and 103-10 alone while the governing provision, s 116-60, is not cited, leaving that material claim only partially verifiable from the cited set.

judge_output.summary: Impeccably sourced to captured primary legislation, but it misses s 116-60 (misappropriation rule), wrongly holds the stolen $50,000 does not reduce proceeds, and so reaches the wrong final figure ($830,000 instead of $780,000).

    extract (page read): ## [![](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/images/tiny-austlii.gif)](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/) Commonwealth Consolidated Acts \[ [Index](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/)\] \[ [Table](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/index.html#s102.5)\] \[ [Search](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinoform.pl)\] \[ [Search this Act](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinoform.pl/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/)\] \[ [Notes](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/notes.html)\] \[ [Noteup](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/sinosrch.pl?query=cth+consol_act+itaa1997240+s102.5)\] \[ [Previous](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s102.3.html)\] \[ [Next](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s102.6.html)\] \[ [Download](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/cgi-bin/download.cgi/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240)\] \[ [Help](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/help/legis-help.html)\] * * * ### INCOME TAX ASSESSMENT ACT 1997 - SECT 102.5 **Assessable income includes net capital gain** (1) Your assessable income includes your [net capital gain](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain) (if any) for the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year). You work out your [net capital gain](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain)in this way: Working out your [net capital gain](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain) Step 1. Reduce the \\* capital gains you made during the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) by the \\* capital losses (if any) you made during the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) as follows: (a) first, reduce any \\* deferred [non-residential capital gains](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#non-residential_capital_gain); (b) then, reduce any \\* deferred [residential capital gains](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#residential_capital_gain); (c) then, reduce any \\* [non-residential capital gains](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#non-residential_capital_gain); (d) then, reduce any \\* [residential capital gains](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#residential_capital_gain). Note 1: Indexation may apply in relation to working out your capital gains: see Divisions 110 and 114. Note 2: Some provisions of [this Act](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#this_act) (such as Divisions 104 and 118) permit or require you to disregard certain capital gains or losses when working out your [net capital gain](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain). Subdivision 152 \- B permits you, in some circumstances, to disregard a capital gain made from a CGT event happening to a CGT asset you [held](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#held) for at least 15 years. Note 3: If you have more than one capital gain within a category mentioned in [paragraph](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.60.html#paragraph)(a), (b), (c) or (d), you can choose the order in [which](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#which) you reduce them. Step 2\. Apply any previously unapplied \\* [net capital losses](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_loss) from earlier [income years](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) to [further](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#further) reduce the amounts (if any) remaining after the reduction of \\* capital gains [under](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) step 1. [Make](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#make) the [further](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#further) reductions in the same order as mentioned in step 1. Note: Section 102 \- 15 explains how to apply [net capital losses](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_loss). Step 3. Apply any quarantined amount referred to in [paragraph](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.60.html#paragraph)26 \- 155(1)(b) you have for the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) to reduce the amounts (if any) of any \\* deferred [residential capital gains](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#residential_capital_gain) remaining after the reduction of \\* capital gains [under](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) step 2. Step 4. Apply any quarantined amount referred to in [paragraph](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.60.html#paragraph)26 \- 155(1)(b) you have for the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) remaining after step 3 to reduce the amounts (if any) of any \\* [residential capital gains](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#residential_capital_gain) remaining after the reduction of \\* capital gains [under](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) step 2. Step 5. Reduce by the \\* discount percentage [each](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#each) amount of any \\* discount capital gain remaining after the application of steps 1 to 4. Note: Only some entities can have discount capital gains, and only if they have capital gains from certain CGT assets acquired at least a year before making the gains: see Division 115\. Step 6. If any of your \\* capital gains (whether or not they are \\* discount capital gains) remaining after step 5 qualify for any of the small [business](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#business) concessions in Subdivisions 152 \- C, 152 \- D and 152 \- E, apply those concessions to [each](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#each) of those capital gains as [provided](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#provide) for in those Subdivisions. Note 1: The basic conditions for getting these concessions are in Subdivision 152 \- A. Note 2: Subdivision 152 \- C does not apply to CGT events J2, J5 and J6. In addition, Subdivision 152 \- E does not apply to CGT events J5 and J6. Step 7. Add up the amounts of any \\* capital gains remaining after step 6. The sum is your [net capital gain](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain)for the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year). Note: For exceptions and modifications to these rules: see section 102 \- 30\. (2) However, if during the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year): (a) you became bankrupt; or (b) you were released from debts [under](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) a law relating to bankruptcy; any \\* [net capital loss](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_loss) you made for an earlier [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) [must](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.15.html#must) be disregarded in working out whether you made a \\* [net capital gain](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#net_capital_gain) for the [income year](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#income_year) or a later one. (3) [Subsection](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s87.70.html#subsection)(2) applies even though your bankruptcy is annulled if: (a) the annulment happens [under](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) section [74](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ba1966142/s74.html) of the [Bankruptcy Act 1966](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/ba1966142/); and (b) [under](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#under) the composition or [scheme](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s995.1.html#scheme) of arrangement concerned, you were, [will](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#will) be or may be released from debts from [which](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/au/legis/cth/consol_act/itaa1997240/s28.5.html#which) you would have been released if instead you had been discharged from the bankruptcy. * * * **AustLII:** [Copyright Policy](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/austlii/copyright.html) **\|** [Disclaimers](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/austlii/disclaimers.html) **\|** [Privacy Policy](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/austlii/privacy.html) **\|** [Feedback](https://www5.austlii.edu.au/austlii/feedback.html)
